speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting supplementary estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1963, was presented by Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance), read by Mr. Speaker to the house, and referred to the committee of supply.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMMEDIATE IMPLEMENTATION OF SALARY REVISIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMMEDIATE IMPLEMENTATION OF SALARY REVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in further reference to the motion I have just made I should like to make a brief statement. After careful consideration the government has approved the recommendations of the treasury board that salary revisions be implemented at once for the employees comprising the second, third and fourth groups in the cyclical salary review program, and that wage adjustments for prevailing rate employees, consideration of which has been deferred for some months, be also put into effect as soon as the paying authorities can make the necessary arrangements.
In accordance with the principles underlying the cyclical salary review policy, the revisions will be effective from the dates as of which the pay research bureau collected the data on which they are based, that is to say:
(a)	In the case of the clerical, administrative, accounting and professional support group, October 1, 1961;
(b)	in the case of the hospital group, January 1, 1962;
(c)	in the case of the penitentiary and police group, April 1, 1962. The prevailing rate wage adjustments will be effective from the dates recommended by the Department of Labour in each case.
Provision has not been made for the increased expenditure involved in the government's decision in the fiscal year 1962-63 in the estimates which have been tabled in the House of Commons and, consequently, a supplementary estimate in the amount of $30 million to augment the general salaries vote,
from which funds will be allotted to departmental votes, has just been tabled. Some 60,000 employees will be receiving increases as a result of action on the three cyclical groups. The number of prevailing rate employees who will receive wage adjustments cannot readily be calculated accurately, but it is estimated at between 5,000 and 6,000.
Consistently with the cyclical salary review policy, statistics are presently being collected by the pay research bureau on which revisions for the fifth group in the cycle will be based. This group embraces the postal, customs and immigration classes, the crafts, building custodial and maintenance classes, and a large number of other classes which were not included in the first four groups. When the civil service commission has considered the data bearing on this fifth group, it will make recommendations for revisions to the government to be effective as of October 1, 1962.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMMEDIATE IMPLEMENTATION OF SALARY REVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think members of the house will have been pleased to hear the minister's announcement regarding pay increases for the civil service although they will not be surprised, because this announcement apparently has already been made outside the house in the columns of the press, indeed before the civil service organization officers, according to reports, had been informed of it.
We on this side of the house, while welcoming the minister's announcement, cannot help but recall that the original pay freeze instituted by the government, which was imposed without following the procedure laid down under section 7 of the Civil Service Act, was in our view unjustified because at that time it forced civil servants to make a contribution to the government's austerity program, which no other occupations were being asked to undertake. The government, having taken that step, is now at this date making what I assume are amends for an action which should not have been taken in the first place.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMMEDIATE IMPLEMENTATION OF SALARY REVISIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF U.N. RESOLUTION FOR WORLD CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 16 I answered a question in the house concerning a resolution adopted in the second, which is the economic, committee of the United Nations general assembly calling for a United Nations conference on trade and development. There were serious difficulties at that time over the timing of the conference, and hon. members will recall that in the committee Canada supported the majority vote in favour of that resolution but major trading nations, including the United States, Britain, Japan and some of the important European economic community countries, voted against it. Twenty three countries abstained. Since it was essential that the major trading nations participate in the United Nations conference if it was to be of practical benefit to developing countries, the Canadian delegation with other delegations has worked strenuously during the past three weeks in an endeavour to resolve the differences about the timing of the conference.
I am pleased to be able to inform the house that on Saturday last at a plenary meeting of the United Nations an amendment to the resolution sponsored by Canada and Peru was accepted and led to the virtually unanimous adoption of the revised resolution by the general assembly. The voting was 91 in favour, none against, and one abstention. The text as approved now commands the support of Britain, the United States, Japan, the common market countries and the 23 countries which abstained in committee.
The original resolution recommended to the economic and social council that it convene the conference not later than September, 1963. The resolution as now adopted recommends to the economic and social council that it convene, after consideration of preparatory work, a United Nations conference on trade and development as soon as possible after the 36th session of ECOSOC, which is July, 1963, but in no event later than early 1964, taking into account the view expressed by a large number of delegations that the conference should be convened not later than September, 1963 as well as the view of other delegations that the conference be held in July, 1964.

Questions
I emphasize that this United Nations conference on trade and development is fully consistent with the Prime Minister's proposal in London which has resulted in the calling of an early meeting of GATT ministers. The GATT ministerial meeting will have as its primary purpose the laying of a foundation for a new round of tariff negotiations and for the reduction of other barriers between the members of GATT. These negotiations would aim at expanding opportunities for world trade and would take advantage of new far-reaching tariff negotiating authority of the United States. The GATT efforts to find solutions to many of the same problems which would be considered in the wider forum of the United Nations will complement and support the broader effort. The importance and urgency of these problems, particularly as they relate to trading interests of developing countries, are such as to require their continued attention in the United Nations, GATT and in other international forums concerned with world trade. Far from there being any conflict between GATT initiatives and the United Nations conference, the Canadian government hopes the two approaches will reinforce each other and thereby increase the prospect for early solutions to the problems of world trade.
We are hopeful that this conference, after careful preparation, will be a working conference from which will emerge positive proposals for concrete solutions for the expansion of trade, particularly for the developing countries. It has not been easy to bring about this compromise in the United Nations and I should like to pay special tribute to Senator F. M. Blois and, of course, the other members of the Canadian delegation for their efforts which have resulted in the adoption of this resolution practically on a unanimous basis.

subtopic: STUDY OF DUTCH ELM DISEASE
STUDY OF DUTCH ELM DISEASE
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of Forestry undertaken a study of the prevalence of Dutch elm disease in Canada and, if so, what is the result of such study? [Mr. Nesbitt.l
2.	What is the federal government doing to eradicate Dutch elm disease?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of Forestry
subtopic: STUDY OF DUTCH ELM DISEASE
speechtext:
1. The
Department of Forestry has undertaken a comprehensive program of surveys and research on the Dutch elm disease and definite procedures are recommended to reduce the destructiveness of this serious disease.
It has been demonstrated that control measures involving the removal of diseased and dead trees and spraying of healthy trees with insecticides can keep losses to tolerable levels. Where these measures are not implemented, however, the disease is expected to continue to kill elms for many years in areas where it now occurs, namely, western New Brunswick and southern Quebec and Ontario, and to spread to other areas; but it is unlikely that it will eliminate elms from our landscape.
Intensive research is in progress to determine how the disease develops in infected trees and on chemotherapy to find improved measures of control. Co-operative studies with Department of Agriculture scientists have resulted in the development of elms apparently resistant to the disease. These trees are presently being critically tested to determine the degree of resistance.
2.	It is unlikely that the Dutch elm disease can ever be completely eradicated. The disease is now well established over extensive areas of Canada and the United States and under these conditions it is impossible to remove all sources of infection. The present program in many cities and park regions is one of sanitation which calls for early detection and removal of infected trees. In cities where these programs have been rigidly applied losses have been reduced to tolerable levels (e.g., Fredericton, N.B.).
The federal government is assisting in control programs by providing technical assistance and guidance in methods and procedures of disease control. Extensive continuing surveys are carried out to define the limits and seriousness of the disease and to provide other information essential for timely control operations.

maintopic: * CANADIAN REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING APPLICATION OF U.S. LABOUR LAWS TO SHIPS

The jurisdiction of the United States national labour relations board is being made the subject of review by the United States supreme court when it considers later this month a series of cases known as the Empresa cases. and are registered by, a foreign nation; and (3) are engaged in the foreign commerce of the United States.

It is a customary practice of the supreme court not to confirm the granting of the application for leave to file until the actual day of the hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Revelsloke):
Has the Department of Forestry received reports of damage to seedlings in plantation and reforestation areas of coastal British Columbia and, if so, what is the department doing to remedy such conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
In recent years approximately 200,000 acres of plantations have been established in British Columbia and as a result insects and diseases attacking small seedlings have received a great deal of attention. Currently the most destructive insect pest is a weevil. This insect has always been present in the British Columbia forests but at low numbers under natural conditions. When areas are cut over or burned and then replanted the weevil shows a marked increase in numbers and causes extensive losses by feeding on planted seedlings. The solution to this problem appears to be one of management. Practical measures of control which will be tested are
Questions
delayed slash burning and more timely planting to avoid weevil attack, and the use of nurse crops to divert the weevils from valuable planted seedlings. A severe outbreak of sweetfern blister rust has been discovered in Bishop and Monterey pine plantings on Vancouver island. This rust occurs on native pines in the region but has never been destructive. The discovery makes doubtful the success of exotic pines in this area and future plantings have been suspended until more is known about the disease. Precautionary measures have been taken to prevent introduction of the rust to regions of the world where Bishop and Monterey pines are native.
Damage to young Douglas fir plantations as a result of browsing by heavy deer populations has been reported to the Department of Forestry by industrial foresters. At the request of the British Columbia tree farm licence committee, the Department of Forestry has initiated a co-operative study, which showed that extreme damage occurs only in small local areas, such as watersheds, where hunting is not permitted. This damage can be found especially throughout tree farm licence areas in southern Vancouver island. Nevertheless, even in areas of heavy damage, the predicted losses in growth are not sufficient to warrant expensive control measures, since they indicate a reduction of only 3 per cent in volume production during an 80 year rotation. Long term studies of browsing damage are being maintained to permit assessment of any changes in trends.
Mortality in fall plantings of Douglas fir seedlings has recently been reported. The Department of Forestry has assigned a tree physiologist to the study of planting stock in an effort to provide basic information on plant-water relationships, root growth, and transpiration patterns of this species. This information will assist in developing improved planting methods and reduction in this mortality.

Question No. 1,09 7-Mr. Marcoux:
1.	What is the average period of time between the receipt by the national film board of accounts from production companies and their payment?
2.	Has any action been taken by the government to hasten the payment of such accounts?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: PAYMENT OF ACCOUNTS BY NATIONAL FILM BOARD
speechtext:
The national film board advises as follows:
1.	The board deals with production companies in the following areas:
(a)	Production of motion picture film,
(b)	Purchase of motion picture prints,
(c)	The provision of motion picture services. An examination of the last two years'
transactions reveals that the average period of time between the receipt by the board of accounts from production companies and the payment thereof is:
(a)	Production of films-an average of 16 days (this leaves out those instances where the terms of the contract have not been met by the producer and further correspondence is necessary. In certain instances matters have to be referred to third parties, i.e. government department sponsors).
(b)	Purchase of prints-the average time is 5 days to 2 weeks. The 2-week time period may be necessary when matters may be referred again to third parties, i.e. sponsors.
(c)	Motion picture service-the average time is one month. Such services are subject to subjective judgment and must be approved by the production personnel involved before clerical routine can begin.
2.	It is felt that the payment of accounts is effected within a reasonable amount of time in view of the nature of the business transacted.

1. Has a national committee on pesticides in agriculture been formed in Canada?

Questions
2. Have any recommendations of this committee been reported and, if so, what are these recommendations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
1. A national committee on pesticide use in agriculture has been formed as a subcommittee of the national co-ordinating committee on agricultural services. The national co-ordinating committee consists of federal and provincial deputy ministers of agriculture and deans of agricultural colleges. The subcommittee on pesticide use is composed of representatives of the departments of national health and welfare, northern affairs and national resources, and agriculture; agricultural colleges, provincial departments of agriculture, and the Canadian chemical industry.
2. Recommendations of the committee reported to the national co-ordinating committee on agricultural services form a basis for a co-ordinated approach to pesticide use in Canada for the guidance of the federal and provincial departments of agriculture. To date these have pertained to:
(a)	The co-ordination and dissemination of available information on pesticide use,
(b)	principles and criteria which may be employed in drafting local recommendations for pesticide use, and
(c)	the need for additional research on pesticides and their use.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, December 7, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-94, to provide for the establishment of an Atlantic development board-Mr. Flemming (Vic-toria-Carleton)-Mr. Chown in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose the other day I was speaking about one great project that is being developed in the Atlantic provinces, the Prince Edward Island causeway. Today I would like to deal with a second project, one that will undoubtedly prove to be the biggest tourist attraction that we have or will have in Canada. This is the restoration of the fortress built by the French government in the early eighteenth century at Louisburg on Cape Breton island.
To illustrate the magnitude of the undertaking that is being carried out I would ask hon. members to visualize a building three quarters as long as parliament building itself and three storeys high. That will be one of the buildings to be placed on the restored fortress site.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What has that got to do with the bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. member will compose himself in patience he will probably have an answer. I mention the restoration of Louisburg as an example of the type of project that can be developed in the Atlantic provinces. Within a radius of 800 miles we have a natural market of 80 million people

Atlantic Development Board to attract to my native area, and I suggest that any project such as Louisburg, with the beneficial results it is bound to bring, should point the way to one of the functions of the Atlantic development board; that is to maintain liaison with those interested in tourist promotion in the Atlantic provinces and also with those interested in it here, namely the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, from the standpoint of administration of attractive places, the people looking after national historic sites and parks, and the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The hon. member for Vancouver East may not have very much interest in Louisburg, but in 1745 and again in 1758 events occurred there which were a turn of the hinge of Canadian history, for this mammoth fortress was the key to effective control of both the St. Lawrence waterway and the eastern seaboard of Canada and the United States. Furthermore, it has had something to do with the establishment of the riding from which I come, for Halifax was founded in 1749 as the English-Yankee counterpoise to the threat from Louisburg. I hope hon. members will play up in this house the $12 million investment that is going to be made in that portion of Cape Breton island, for it will bring with it the concomitants of a hotel development, a resource development, a boating development and other recreational developments, and will be one of the great boons not only to the island of Cape Breton but to the whole economy of the Atlantic provinces.
Broadening the theme somewhat, Mr. Chairman, one of the interesting things about development in the past has been the special allocation of $300,000 in the last three or four years to promote tourism for the Atlantic area in the nearby United States market. This has paid off very handsomely. As I said before, history has been one of our great natural resources in the maritimes, and since 1957 the government has certainly seized upon this resource and developed it with both skill and vigour. I have in my hands figures issued recently by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources showing the number of visitors to various national parks and major historic sites across Canada. There are such significant increases as 80,000 more visitors to the Cape Breton highlands this year, 233,000 to the Anne of Green Gables country, 33,000 to Signal Hill in St. John's, Newfoundland, and almost 12,000 to the Halifax Citadel. Therefore I say that in my opinion the Atlantic development board and its members should keep in close liaison with the departments in Ottawa which administer


or promote the great national historic sites that we have in abundance in Atlantic Canada.
Turning to another point, Mr. Chairman, if I may, there have been various suggestions as to how the problems of Atlantic Canada could be most usefully tackled. There has been a school of thought which advocates that this be done by a department of government. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned this the other day, and I believe during the election campaign the hon. member for Davenport proffered this as the solution of the Liberal party. I was very pleased to see another Liberal, the hon. member for inverness-Richmond, reject outright the notion of establishing a department of Atlantic affairs. If any more backward step could be imagined in the House of Commons I hardly know what it could be. It would almost set us apart from the rest of Canada as either a special institution or a plantation, and I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and those other hon. members who advocate such a department will quickly switch their tune if they think of the pride of the people involved in my particular region, and come to appreciate that an advisory board is a much better approach to Atlantic problems.
I have already dealt with some of those things which I consider should be functions of the board. There is the development of those things which we have, for example our historical heritage, rather than following the will-o'-the-wisp things that we have not. There are at least two provinces in Canada which have tried the experiment of spending large amounts of taxpayers' money for the development of industry, with very little success. The trail of smoke from the bonfires of the taxpayers' money and the deficit operations of crown corporations in Newfoundland and Saskatchewan should surely indicate that government is not primarily at its best in the field of business. None the less, this does not prevent a board such as we are considering today from performing useful functions, particularly in its advice on measures and projects.
I have an interesting quotation from one of the spokesmen at the recent meeting of the Atlantic provinces economic council at Fredericton, Claude K. Howse, Newfoundland representative of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. Here is how he treats the problem:
The hoard must be empowered to "advise on measures and projects" in both the public and private sectors. Certainly, provincial governments and their agencies should have access to the new federal agency to assist in the development of public facilities, such as transportation and power generation and transmission. A province should

also be able to apply to the board for assistance in the establishment of industrial estates or similar projects designed to encourage industrialization directly. But just as important, it will be necessary for the board to be in a position to encourage and assist the private sector, either directly or through the provincial governments, in new resource exploration and development, and in the location of cornerstone plants, in the development, in primary resource industry areas, of secondary industry related industrially or economically to the primary industry, and other enterprises which can have an impact on the course of economic progress.
I thought his words so sensible, Mr. Chairman, that I have taken the liberty of putting them into the debate. Finally, sir, there is a point which I hope the new board will consider. Again I return to the theme that we should build up those things that we have, rather than follow will-o'-the-wisp [DOT]endeavours that will simply represent a costly wasting of taxpayers' money.
One thing I would like to see is the enhancement of one of the great industries in the Atlantic provinces; that is, the diversification of the Sydney steel plant operations. This would not only be of great benefit to Cape Breton island but it would also be of special benefit to a large industry in my own riding, the Halifax shipyards, which would be able to use-if my hopes in this respect are realized-rolled steel from an expanded Sydney plant for the many excellent ships it builds for public and private enterprise.
These are some of the thoughts that pass through my mind. I certainly will support this imaginative proposal. I have great faith in the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance. I know they will choose personnel who will transform the words we are considering this afternoon into a magic which will bring new hope and happiness to my area.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a sad coincidence that on the very day we are discussing in this house a matter pertaining to the Atlantic region it should become my duty to pay homage to the memory of one who spent a lifetime of tireless effort for the improvement of the maritimes and of New Brunswick especially.
On Saturday, December 8 Mr. Allison Dysart passed from this life into eternity. The belief that we are to be rewarded in the next life in the same measure as we have served in this one will, no doubt, be of great consolation to his family and his myriad friends. His passing closes another era in the history of New Brunswick. He was a native son of Kent county, the county I am proud to represent in this house. He was premier of New Brunswick from 1935 to 1940, and will always be remembered in the province as the first to bring in legislation for the
Atlantic Development Board comfort of the aged. I know that hon. gentlemen on all sides will join me in extending to Mrs. Dysart and the family our sincere sympathy.
It is not my intention to retard in any way the progress of legislation which could be of assistance to the Atlantic region, for we all know that assistance of any kind has been long overdue. I am in accord with the suggestions of some of the hon. members who have spoken that we should let the past rest in peace and look to the future, but it is inevitable that we take a good look at the present, also, and what we see in the maritimes is not so encouraging. Thank God we have in the Atlantic provinces a people who are hardy and industrious and who have an inexhaustible reserve of initiative in surmounting the obstacles in the way of making what we call a bare living. I am referring to the farmers and fishermen who make up a big part of our population of the maritimes. These are the people who work from daylight to dark to bring up and educate their families, and they are doing a herculean job of it considering the disadvantages they encounter.
As one who knows, Mr. Chairman, I say that the fishermen have to expose thousands of dollars worth of equipment and gear to the elements, not to mention their own lives, in order to eke out a living from the sea. Not infrequently they leave orphans and widows behind. We know that an indemnity insurance exists, with respect to boats and lobster traps, but such provisions as these do not cover the loss suffered by widows and orphans or comfort them in their distress. Another thing we must realize is this. It is extremely hard to persuade a man to pay insurance premiums when he is hard pressed for money needed by his own family.
One could go on and on when speaking of matters which concern the fishing industry, the condition of some wharves, the necessity for dredging channels to improve the fishing and shipping industries in the maritimes, and so on. When we note that the value of the lobster fishing alone to the Atlantic region is in the vicinity of $15 million a year, hon. members can realize how important the fishing industry is to this whole area.
It is a well known fact that if the population of the maritimes were larger the individual burden of taxation would be lighter. The construction and maintenance of highways in the rural areas, of which the Atlantic region is mostly comprised, costs as much per mile as it does in a thickly populated area. The same applies to all other public services. We must face the fact that our people, anxious to equip their children for

Atlantic Development Board the future, must see that they get an education. The cost of schools and their staffing in rural areas puts a tremendous load on the municipalities which, in turn, must tax the farm properties to a point which makes it almost impossible for the farmers to survive. Some move away, and the additional burden falls on those who remain.
Until a few years ago the farmers were not too greatly affected by the situation, for they could always rely on income from pulp-wood cut on their wood lots during the slack season. This furnished them with a ready source of cash, but unfortunately this market is no longer available. It is discouraging to reflect that something which is absolutely essential if our youth are to be prepared for the future is indirectly the cause of many of them having to migrate to the industrialized sections of upper Canada. The maritime provinces, the birthplace of confederation, made many sacrifices to make Canada a nation and are still contributing royally of their most cherished potential, their youth.
This is the situation which exists in most of the rural parts of the maritimes. What is needed to stimulate the economy and relieve unemployment is direct action on the part of this government by devoting a larger share of the capital expenditures to the construction of public works and harbours in the region, and by finding ways and means of lightening the tax load at the municipal level. If this were done the Atlantic development board would have time to develop long term measures toward a stable and prosperous economy in the region.
May I suggest that if this government had paid more attention to the requests and advice of our Atlantic premiers we would be well on our way. I think in all fairness we deserve more than a board which is to function in an advisory capacity only, based in importance on a maritime standard of remuneration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to say initially that I agree wholeheartedly with the comments of the hon. member for Halifax-the taller member for Halifax-in what he said about the development of the old fortress of Louisburg. My hope is that this will be a great and continuing tourist attraction. As the hon. member knows, we have many such sites in the Atlantic provinces to which tourists are coming in increasing numbers, and anything that this or any other government can do to make these sites more attractive is to be commended.
On Friday the Minister of National Revenue referred to the $3,000 proposed as an honorarium for the chairman of the Atlantic development board as a ridiculous figure, and

announced his intention to move an amendment to change it. Mr. Chairman, this is an important point. The bill which is before us came to this house as a carefully considered piece of legislation. We may be sure that the minister weighed every provision and every phrase with the utmost care. In doing so he approved the figure of $3,000 as an appropriate honorarium for the chairman of this board.
I suggest that this figure is important to this committee, because it gives us a good idea of the government's opinion of the work to be done by the Atlantic development board. This board is not to be very active. It is presumably, to meet three or four times a year, and the government is fixing an honorarium commensurate with the activities of the board. Similarly, in fixing honoraria for the other members the government is giving due attention to its view of how active this board is to be, for it has assigned to those other members no remuneration whatsoever.
Now, sir, the minister has seen that this figure of $3,000 discloses the true nature of this board. Immediately he tries to becloud the fact with candour. He comes to this committee and says that this figure, of course, is "ridiculous." Moreover, by suggesting that the honorarium will be raised he now falls into inconsistency, for he has not yet proposed any honoraria whatsoever for the other members of the board. I do not know just how much the minister means to imply by his word "ridiculous", but if the chairman is to receive some such figure as $10,000 or $12,000, surely the other four members ought to receive payment also.
Last Thursday and Friday we were exhorted by the minister to be enthusiastic. I think only the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg displayed what one might consider the proper degree of joy and thankfulness for this proposed legislation. Not even the hon. member for Halifax, in his balanced remarks just now concluded, came up to the level that the minister suggested.
We on this side, sir, believe that the minister is quite sincere in his zeal for this bill, yet I can assure you that in our expressions of disappointment we are equally sincere. This bill creates a part time board which is to study certain matters and advise an unspecified minister. Evidently the explanation of the misunderstanding is that our expectations were very different from the expectations of the minister. Our expectations were far higher than his. We expected more from this government than even he did.
As any member of this committee who has had any special reason to be interested in programs for surplus labour areas knows, in certain European countries such as Great

Britain, West Germany, France, Belgium, Denmark, Sweden and Italy there are under way important programs dealing with the problem of surplus labour areas. Four different kinds of regional development tactics or devices have been employed; loans, grants, tax incentives and government assistance in site improvement and plant construction. Of these four the first two, loans and grants, have been used most frequently and are apparently by far the most successful. Loans and grants are often used to supplement each other. A company will be given a loan at a very low interest rate for part of its capital needs. For example, in Belgium the interest rate is geared to the acceleration or deceleration of the national economy, so that the interest rate in a period of depression might be as low as 1 per cent. The other two devices, tax incentives and site improvements, have not been used so extensively. Indeed, only Great Britain and Belgium have used site improvement and plant construction to any considerable extent.
Now, sir, knowing that these methods have been tried in other countries, and knowing that a great deal of thought has been given in the United States to this matter of surplus labour areas, we had hoped that this government would come to this house, and eventually to this committee, with an elaborated program for the Atlantic provinces. However, we have not had such a program put before us, and I wish to assure the minister through you, sir, that the disappointment which we express is entirely genuine.
A fifth device has been mooted. I almost hesitate to mention it; I do not wish to arouse some members opposite, because I have noticed that this is a very delicate point with them. I refer to labour migration assistance. Whenever one mentions labour migration assistance, or indeed whenever one mentions the name of the hon. member for Davenport, one can generally count on an eruption from certain seats on the other side of the house. Unfortunately no one will rise to that bait now.
You may recall, sir, that in the report of the Gordon commission there is a suggestion on pages 412 and 413 that if various methods for dealing with labour surplus are not effective, then the government is to intervene to assist people in moving to towns and places where they may obtain employment. After a great deal of exclamation from campaign orators and from the government benches in this house, the government has finally decided that Mr. Gordon may have been correct after all. So we now find a bill before this house, Bill No. C-83, respecting industrial change and manpower adjustment, which provides that the minister may make an agreement-
Atlantic Development Board
-to provide for the payment by Canada of a labour mobility incentive consisting of a contribution in respect of the cost incurred by such province, person or both, as the case may be, for the transportation of workers and their dependants to an area in Canada where employment is available.
The ultimate conversion of the government to the view expressed earlier by the hon. member for Davenport has been commented on in the press. I have in my hand an editorial from the Moncton Transcript which I think the committee will find entertaining. One paragraph says:
The Introduction of a "labour mobility" scheme to assist in the relocation of workers who become unemployed as a result of industrial changes is probably a worth while, but somewhat superficial attempt at tackling a problem which has particular application in the maritimes.
But beyond this there is the fact that the Progressive Conservatives, who are introducing the new legislation, were the party who criticized most vigorously a similar suggestion in the report of the Gordon royal commission.
Then the editor goes on to divert himself with speculation concerning the joy that this particular bill must give to the heart of the hon. member for Davenport. So, sir, labour migration assistance is a fifth method that has at times been used. It has not yet been used extensively. The principal country using it has been Sweden, but soon we will be able to add Canada to Sweden in this regard.
The minister has assured us that we should be happy with this board. Perhaps we should take him seriously, sir, for after all he knows more about the thinking of this government than we do. He knows more about how slowly it progresses in dealing with serious problems. If he comes to this committee and says, as he has, that this bill represents a great step forward in the thinking of the government, then I suggest we should believe what he says.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall only say a few words to mention that this morning, I came across a large headline in the Evangeline, the newspaper from Moncton:
Is the Atlantic board serious?
Indeed, after having heard the bombastic words and the numerous speeches made on the setting up of commissions and boards, we may wonder if those agencies are created to organize something which will merely

Atlantic Development Board be a subject for discussion or something which will bring adequate revenues in the Atlantic provinces.
I suggest that the journalists are right in asking whether the board is serious.
The member who had the floor before me just referred to the dilatoriness of government agencies. Well, I have discovered in the Glassco report that not very long ago, under the Liberal government, works had been provided for at Port-aux-Basques. Here is an example of a completely abnormal situation:
In accordance with the terms of union of Newfoundland and Canada, a freight and passenger steamship service is maintained between North Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Port-aux-Basques, Newfoundland. The program was initiated in 1951 and called for the construction of a ferry and docks and terminal facilities in each province. Three separate agencies of government and several firms of consulting engineers participated in this work which, as a result of a series of costly errors, was not completed until 1959. The ferry, when built, could not be docked at the newly constructed facilities at Port-aux-Basques. The final solution, reached after calling in an experienced adviser from the United Kingdom, required extensive dredging and channel rectification. The total costs exceeded $20 million.
At that time, we saw the tremendous importance of those commissions. And, of course, once again the companies were the ones to benefit from that situation whereas the individual has not been favoured. When we ask the government to increase family allowances, we are told there is not enough money. Nevertheless, the Atlantic development board will submit its recommendations, and if we have no money, if we have deficits of $700 million, how shall we be able to consider seriously in this house the recommendations of those agencies?
I am not against the development board, but I would like to see it bring about results. I am afraid that this board, which we are now allowed to discuss, will be like the various boards set up under the Liberals and that it will take eight years before it can be of any real benefit.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the one concrete thing about this bill we have before us is that it provides that a minister is to be designated to deal with the board and that the minister may refer to the board from time to time certain specific projects for study and recommendation. I should like to take a few minutes now to draw to the minister's attention two or three specific projects which would be of tremendous benefit to the economy of my own riding and also to that of the province of Newfoundland.

The first project I wish to bring to the minister's attention is the development of a free port or transshipment port at Mortier bay. This is a dream that is 50 years old. Recently a company has been formed and I understand that surveys have been made not only by the company but by a departmental committee and that already in the files of the Department of Public Works or some other department, probably the Department of Transport, there is information indicating that Mortier bay is a strategically situated focal point along the world's trade routes. I understand that the studies and surveys that have been carried out prove that the harbour is very satisfactory, and apparently all that is needed to bring this project into being is to bring together the commercial interests involved in such a way that they can get started on the project.
If this project came into being it would be a tremendous development that would benefit not only Newfoundland but all of Canada because it envisages goods being brought into Mortier bay, processed there and shipped out to other parts of the world. As I said earlier, the strategic position of Mortier bay makes this project feasible. I also understand that it has the blessing of our friends from the prairie provinces because the Hudson bay route association is most interested in having more wheat shipped through Churchill and stored at Mortier bay for transshipment. As soon as the new board comes into being I would ask the minister to refer this specific project to them for immediate study.
The second project I would ask the minister to refer to the board is the development of hydroelectric power at bay d'Espoir which is in my own riding. At bay d'Espoir we are fortunate in having a potential of half a million horsepower which can be developed at tidewater and the consumption of only 70,000 horsepower is required to make the project commercially feasible. A few years ago the project came within a hair's breadth of being realized but it was found impossible to get the companies having an option for this amount of power together at the right time. By the time the last person was brought into the agreement the first person who had wanted power withdrew from the project because of not being able to wait any longer, and that is why the development did not take place.
There is no doubt that the development of this power at bay d'Espoir would transform the whole economy of my riding and would be of tremendous assistance to the economy of the whole province. I hope the minister will refer this project to the board at once.

The hon. member for Halifax mentioned earlier the restoration of the old fort at Louisburg. I would suggest to the minister the board study a similar project, namely the restoration and development of Castle Hill at Placentia which is the old historic French capital of my province. 1 would recommend also the study of similar sites in the province. Such developments could be of great benefit to our tourist industry.
In this connection, I would ask the minister to have a study made of the feasibility of finding a more suitable terminal for Canadian National Railways. As the minister is probably aware, the eastern terminal is at Argentia, which is a military base leased to the United States authorities for a period of 90 years. We have been told that a new ferry is to be built which will ply between the east coast of Newfoundland and North Sydney in Nova Scotia. The Newfoundland terminal will be located at Argentia. There are many reasons why this is an unsatisfactory place for the terminal, not only for this particular ferry but for the whole coastal service operated by the railway along the south coast. I know that representations have been made to the government indicating that there are other sites which are much better suited to this proposal. Since our tourist industry is becoming of such importance, and since it ties in with the development of the fort at Castle Hill, I would suggest further consideration be given to this matter. Since the government actually owns the railway service in Newfoundland and the railway management would do what the government wanted in this respect, I would suggest that the minister have this board look into this matter of finding a more suitable terminal.
Before I resume my seat, 1 should like to support the representations made by my colleague the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador in respect of the fishing industry which is still of major importance in my province and about which there is a new enthusiasm and a new effort being made to try to put it back on a sound footing. I think one of the main problems in connection with the fishing industry in the promotion of sales in various markets on the mainland. This is probably one other thing that can be looked into. I would remind the minister, too, that in all the years the Conservative party sat in opposition they were very strong proponents of a Canadian merchant fleet. I am one of those who believes that there is a place in our economy for a Canadian owned merchant fleet. This, too, 1 think is a project worthy of study by the development board.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know that the committee is anxious to get on with a
Atlantic Development Board clause by clause study of this measure. However, there are a few remarks I should like to make in connection with this interesting matter that is before us. I can assure you I will only take a very few minutes. Hon. members are familiar with the terms of the resolution, but I would remind them that the throne speech contained this paragraph:
You will be asked to authorize the establishment of an Atlantic development board to advise on measures and projects that will promote the economic development of the Atlantic region of Canada.
The presentation of the resolution preceding Bill No. C-94 has been received with great fanfare in the daily press of the Atlantic region. Large type headlines on the front pages lauding this measure lead the public in the provinces by the Atlantic to believe it is a quick cure-all and to believe that all the economic ills of the area will be resolved forthwith. In this connection, it is realistic and responsible that a somewhat sober note should be injected into the public's mind. They should be reminded that great things will not be accomplished overnight. However, if this legislation does accomplish anything it would be to hold out the hope that eventually the situation will be faced and that improvements will follow. I think this is something the people of the maritime provinces will receive with rightful anticipation after many, many years, and they will hope that finally something will be done about their problems.
This Bill No. C-94 seeks only to set up a board which will provide the government with suggested projects for the improvement of the economy of the area. One might well ask, is this board so vitally needed as the public is being led to believe? The projects that are generally felt to be necessary to bring about a stable economy in the Atlantic provinces do not need to be related to the government or to the people in the maritime provinces by a board established under this bill. The necessary action to bring about improvement in the Atlantic economy can be taken by the government now. There is an abundance of data available compiled by APEC and other groups that can be used to lay the foundation for government action. This data has been available since APEC first started to function. What will a board comprised of a $3,000 a year chairman and five non-indemnified members produce that has not already been produced?
I noted what the minister said on Friday, that the amount of $3,000 was ridiculous and would be bettered, but he did not say by what amount. However, I believe that when you establish a board with a chairman receiving an indemnity of $3,000 a year, it

Atlantic Development Board reveals the fact the government itself is not putting too much confidence in this board. Perhaps, however, the government feels someone who is not concerned about the remuneration will offer his services. The time required to set up this board and for the board to review the data already compiled will further delay government action on the Chignecto complex, the Northumberland strait causeway, the coal mining and fishing industries as well as other phases of the Atlantic economy. These areas require action now, action which only the government can take because of the expenditure of public funds required. What is needed is direct action to provide the public funds with which to commence some of these vital projects and improvements. Following that there can be a planned approach to the development of other projects in order to bring about improvements that are the inherent rights of the people of the Atlantic provinces.
We recognize that Bill C-94 will be approved and passed, but the people of the Atlantic provinces will have to wait to see what benefits will follow the setting up of this board. Personally I sincerely hope and trust that the benefits will accrue without undue delay.
As to the personnel of the board, it is suggested that it should be representative of all the Atlantic provinces and that its members will be fully qualified to advise in those fields in which our economy is lacking. Leadership by government is a most essential factor in achieving the desired results and this leadership should not be delegated to any board or commission. When suggestions or advice are sought by the government, then no delay should be tolerated in reaching decisions.
I am sure I express the hopes and desires of all people in the Atlantic provinces, and of other peoples in the confederation family, when I say there is a sound expectation that the basic economic problems of the area will at last be acted upon and their solution undertaken without further delay. No matter what the political aspects might be, it is not so important who solves these problems or how they are solved, but it is vitally important that their solutions be expedited in order to bring about equal partnership among all regions of Canada.
Hon. members who have already taken part in this debate have told of certain requirements which they feel are necessary in their individual constituencies. They have brought them to the attention of the minister, who in turn will bring them to the attention of the new board when it is constituted. In this regard I only want to mention one thing in particular with respect to the constituency of Northumberland-Miramichi.

I would ask the minister to bring to the attention of the board something that has been under study for some time past, and that is the deepening of the channel of the Miramichi river and the improvement of harbour facilities at the ports of Chatham and Newcastle. As a native maritimer I sincerely hope and trust that at long last we shall get something under way to bring about these things we need so vitally, and I am sure that the minister, who is also a native maritimer, will do his utmost to see that the desired end is achieved. I am one of those who believe that, irrespective of what a government does, it should be commended for those things that are beneficial.
In conclusion I wish to join with my colleague from Kent in expressing regret at the death of Judge Dysart, a former premier of the province of New Brunswick. I also join with him in extending condolences to the family of this great New Brunswicker who has passed on to his just reward after serving his province so well for so many years.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo, as I did likewise to the speech of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador.

Both excellent

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

speechtext:
Both excellent speeches, as the hon. member for Essex East has interjected, and I would like to say a few words in support of the arguments advanced by my tv/o colleagues from Newfoundland because I believe that in their own way, and in a very good and sensible way, they advanced very strong arguments in favour of the establishment of the Atlantic development board.
In his speech the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned two projects that he commended to the minister and asked that they be studied by the board, and I would like to refer to them briefly. He mentioned the establishment of a free port at Mortier bay. This is a project that has been under active promotion for the last several years. It has been studied by various agencies and its importance to the economy of Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces generally cannot be underestimated. Here is where this new board could really do something worth while in undertaking a study of a project such as this and, at the same time, assimilating and co-ordinating the studies and promotions that have gone on before in connection with it. This project has been mentioned in the house on numerous occasions and I hope that the board, when it is set up, will give active study

to the establishment of a free port in Newfoundland which is, as I say, of vital importance not only to that province but to all the Atlantic provinces.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo also referred to the development of hydro power at bay d'Espoir, on the south coast of Newfoundland, and I believe these two projects are related. One is almost dependant on the other. If a free port is established at Mortier bay I believe it will mean the influx of small industries, the establishment of substantial storage facilities, elevators and so on, which would create a demand for additional hydro power that could be supplied by the development of hydro at bay d'Espoir. Then too, with the new techniques for the transmission of hydro power, I believe the development of bay d'Espoir holds tremendous possibilities.
The hon. member also referred to tourism, to the present terminal for the C.N.R. at Argentia, and to the use of this terminal as a terminal for the proposed new ferry which will operate between eastern Newfoundland and the mainland of Nova Scotia. I support the hon. member in these remarks because I believe that, before it is finally decided that Argentia should be the terminal for this all important ferry, further studies should be undertaken, and I think reference should be made to the board to make sure that the Newfoundland terminal for the ferry will be a maximum benefit to the promotion of the tourist industry in our province. I think the hon. gentleman will forgive me for saying the board should certainly give consideration to the advisability of having the eastern terminal closer to the city of St. John's and the concentration of population.
Speaking of tourism I believe the board can provide a tremendous service in co-ordinating efforts of various agencies such as the governments of the provinces, municipal governments, boards of trade and chambers of commerce, in addition to APEC, towards the general promotion of tourism and the promotion of specific projects that would be incentives to tourism. I believe there is a tremendous job to be done here, especially in my own province, and the greatest need is the need of coordination. Everyone seems to be going off in different directions and somebody must coordinate the efforts of all because tourism is very important to the three maritime provinces and to the province of Newfoundland where it holds tremendous possibilities.
In relation to tourism the hon. member referred to historic sites and the development of Louisburg in Cape Breton, and he spoke of the need for similar undertakings in the province of Newfoundland where we have
Atlantic Development Board, many major historic sites. Among the historic sites to which he referred was Castle Hill in Placentia, the historic French capital of Newfoundland. I hope the board will undertake an active consideration of the advisability of developing this site and will recommend to the government that this type of site be developed. Certainly, as I said, not the least of such sites is the one located in Placentia.
My hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador referred in his speech to the fishing industry and the service the board could provide in this particular area. This is a very important area. I am pleased to say the government of Newfoundland has of late been active in this regard. They called a convention of trades people, merchants, fishermen and like-minded people with a view to their coming up with recommendations to the government of the province toward the formation of a new policy on fisheries. The importance of the fisheries to the Atlantic coast of Canada is of course of tremendous significance. I feel that here is certainly an area where the board can really justify its existence by co-ordinating the efforts of various agencies, recommending projects to the government that would be of encouragement to the fishing industry, exploring markets for our fish produce, and of course looking for new markets, ways of improving those markets, and so on.
All these projects-and of course one could go on and name many others-are of tremendous importance to the general development of the Atlantic provinces. But I feel that what is of real importance is the fact that at long last we are about to set up a board which will give real meaning to the development of these various projects and will undertake to work with the very competent Minister of National Revenue, the minister from New Brunswick. I am sure that at long last some of these projects which have been talked about for many years now have a better chance of materializing because we are about to set up this Atlantic development board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know there has been a good deal of debate on the first item of this bill and I will not delay the committee unduly, but I would like to indicate my support for this proposed board. I know that the board is going to be advisory in nature. In our part of Canada we have the Atlantic provinces economic council. This council has done a good deal of commendable research. It has been able to suggest topics that are important to the maritime and Atlantic provinces and I think at times they
2498	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Development Board have indicated the methods which should be adopted if these ideas are to be brought to fruition.
Perhaps one of the difficulties of the Atlantic provinces economic council is that there has been no vehicle whereby the ideas the council may have can be transmitted to the inner circle of government. Perhaps this board we are proposing will be the vehicle that will be able to do that; perhaps it will be sufficient to do the job that is required to be done. Personally I would like to see this board composed of members who are more firmly committed to the task in hand and with a little bit more executive authority than its members are given in this bill. However, when a body of men such as will compose this board turn their attention to the task that has to be accomplished in the Atlantic provinces I hope they will remember that doing what needs to be done in this area is not always a matter of doing something new. It may indeed in large part amount to improving what is already being done. I think there are many things going on in the Atlantic provinces at the moment that are not being conducted in a way that gives the most to the economy of that part of Canada. I hope this board will be able to make suggestions to various divisions of the economy so that these things that are being done will be done more effectively, not only for the people who are directly concerned but also for the area as a whole.
In the constituency from which I come we have a problem to which I hope the board will give serious attention. In 1941-42, during the early years of the second world war, the Americans came to the west coast of Newfoundland and there set up a tremendous air force base. Over a period of 15 or 20 years there was a great deal of construction work carried out there. It was obvious that while this large amount of construction work was going ahead men were going to be drawn from the fishing industry, from the farming industry and other small industries and would go into the construction field where good wages were to be earned. This was the position for a considerable length of time. However, it must have been obvious to all concerned that the time would come when this construction had to cease and the United States base would settle down to normal operations. We have now, on the west coast of Newfoundland, reached that position.
It is very easy, if a fisherman decides he is going to move from the fishing industry into some other type of work, for him to haul his boat up on the beach, lock up his nets and gear in a shed and move on. As I say, it is very easy to do that; but when the time comes for him to move back into the


fishing industry the transformation is not so easy. Here in this section of Newfoundland- and I am referring particularly to the Port-au-Port peninsula-we have hundreds of men who left the fishing industry 20 years ago and worked on the construction of the base at Harmon field. Now that construction has finished and they have to go back to the fishing industry. The going back is rather difficult. To begin with, they do not have the money to set themselves up as individual fishermen. Then, of course, due to the fact that for a number of years there has not been as large a number of fishermen as there might have been, we do not have the fish firms set up there as they have in other parts of Newfoundland or indeed in other parts of Nova Scotia. Here is one problem of labour movement to which I hope this board will pay very serious attention.
While I am referring to the fishing industry, Mr. Chairman, I hope too that this board will pay particular attention to the northern part of Newfoundland. This is a section of Newfoundland where there is almost no industry other than fishing. A few years ago there was considerable employment in forestry-in the logging industry. Employment opportunities in this area have decreased, however, and the result is that here we have one of the few areas in Canada where men make approximately 100 per cent of their total income from fishing. I hope this board will pay particular attention to the problems these men encounter; some of them are peculiar to this particular region.
I believe there is a good deal which could be done in agriculture. Newfoundland is not agricultural country and I suggest it will never be an agricultural province in the sense that other parts of Canada are. Nevertheless, I think it is possible for Newfoundland to provide for itself larger amounts of agricultural products than it is doing now-products of the kind which are normally brought in at the present time from other parts of Canada or other parts of the world. On the west coast of Newfoundland there is a good deal of agriculture carried on mostly in the domain of small vegetables. In the last year or two we have been faced with a difficult problem there in the control of insects. How we are going to overcome this seems beyond the farmer and there is a real need for some expert assistance. The minister is familiar with the difficulty we encounter in the control of insects and forestry. That, of course, affects many more people. Nevertheless, the control of insects in the Robinson's area and the Codroy valley will require a good deal of research.

I do not believe any province such as Newfoundland is going to get very far with economic development until proper means of transportation are provided. Of the approximately 600 miles of trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland, almost 200 are in my own constituency. When we talk about the tourist industry these days we are talking, I think, about people who want to travel from one part of Canada to another by car. People like to come into an area and drive by car over roads which provide comfortable travelling-roads which enable them, too, to go from one place to another in as short a time as possible. One of the real problems in Newfoundland is the inability to complete the trans-Canada highway at an early date. I am one of those who believe-I said this when I was on the other side of the house, I have said it here, and now I say it again -that when the federal government of Canada decided to build the trans-Canada highway they should have decided, by agreement with the provinces, to build that highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to pay for it and maintain it. I think that is what should have been done. I do not think we are too far from the point when we shall be facing a real problem in the maintenance of the trans-Canada highway. Anyway, had the course I advocated been followed I suppose we would not have the trouble we are encountering in Newfoundland at the present time.
It is all very well to talk about the tourist industry in Newfoundland. I believe we have the potential for a great tourist industry. But if people wish to travel by car we have, first of all, to get them on to the island. At the moment there is only one ferry taking cars to the island, though a few cars can come by other boats. And when they get there they have to travel over roads that are not paved. So I would say to the minister that one of the problems which this board should consider in all seriousness is the question of being able to provide for the province of Newfoundland the same road transport facilities as are provided in most of the other provinces. I drive my own car from Corner Brook to Ottawa, sometimes more than once a year, and I have the opportunity to use the trans-Canada highway in some of the other provinces. I do hope the time is not too far distant when I shall have the privilege of driving over roads in Newfoundland which are paved as well as they are in the minister's own province.
Power development is another necessity if we are to promote the establishment of industry and particularly of small industries which, I think, are important to a province such as ours. I do not think we need a very
Atlantic Development Board large number of giant sized industries right across Canada. I think the background of the economy is provided by a large number of smaller businesses employing a few men here, a few there, and so on. But one of the prerequisites to such a development is electric power readily available at a low price. I was glad to hear the comments of my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo and also from the hon. member for St. John's East who mentioned the development of power on the south coast of Newfoundland. There is, indeed, considerable power potential there to be developed and I think this is a project to which the board might well give serious and early attention.
I should like to say a word on vocational training, as it relates to this subject, but since we shall have an opportunity to discuss this matter on another bill which is before the house I shall refrain from speaking at any length at the moment. However, I believe that if industries of various types are to be developed, or if we are to expand the industries which are already operating in the province, we shall have to provide the particular types of training which are so important. In Ontario and in western Canada generally a good deal of technical training has been provided, I believe, for those who work on farms. We, in Newfoundland, need training of this type. Our fishermen will need a special type of training if they are going to earn a living, not as their fathers did, but as fishermen who must operate in modern times. I do hope the board will take an interest in these vocational training programs when it is considering the economic problems of Newfoundland even though other government agencies may be dealing more directly with this particular subject. I have some ideas on vocational training, which is closely allied to my own profession. I do not intend to state them now but I will take advantage of the opportunity which will arise later to say what I think should be done; particularly in the eastern part of Canada.

speechtext:
I hope I shall be forgiven, Mr. Chairman, for taking a few more minutes, but I shall try to be brief. I should like to express appreciation of the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John's East, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, all of whom referred to matters which are of great interest to the province from which I come.
Tourism is extremely important to us. I doubt very much if most of us can visualize the tremendous potential which it has. No doubt it would be difficult for any of us to speak objectively of the attractions of our own provinces, but suffice it to say that when

Atlantic Development Board we assert that Newfoundland offers delightful attractions we are only quoting what so many visitors have told us. But in order for tourism to be the industry which it can be, it is of overwhelming importance that the trans-Canada highway be completed in Newfoundland. The high cost of building this road is placing a very great strain on the government of Newfoundland, and I would stress the importance of the completion of the trans-Canada highway in the Atlantic provinces by the federal government. It is, as I say, of tremendous importance, and it is impossible to overstress this. I would hope that the new board will give serious attention to the matter.
I might also mention in connection with historic sites the interesting discoveries which have been made in L'Anse aux Meadows in northern Newfoundland. The ruins which have been excavated over the past two years seem to prove that there was a Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of the great northern peninsula a thousand years ago. I am no authority on this, but I am told that the authenticity of these ruins has been all but proven. I really do not know whether those who are competent to judge have handed down a final decision, but my latest information is that the ruins seem to be authentic. That area will soon be connected by road. There is a long road up the coast of Newfoundland to within a comparatively few miles of this area. I would hope that the board would pay particular attention to these ruins, where a thousand years ago there was a settlement of Vikings who had sailed across the Atlantic to discover this great nation of Canada which is ours today.
Then the question of trade was mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's East. I believe he referred to marketing. There again I would hope that the board would look carefully into the matter of properly exploiting the markets of the world for the fishery products of the Atlantic provinces, in order to give that proper emphasis to pushing our trade so that a really vigorous policy could be pursued and our fishery products sold in great quantity in the world's markets. May I conclude my few remarks, Mr. Chairman, by hoping that the Atlantic economic development board will provide an instrument of break-through for the hopes and the needs of the people of the Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am quite certain that the minister and a great many other members will be somewhat surprised that I should rise to say a few words on this bill, but I do so for a number of reasons. First of all, I think that a bill which is designed to improve the economic situation of a part of


our great country deserves the support of all areas of the country. Second, no part of Canada has benefited more from the mari-times, or owes more to the maritimes, than my native province of British Columbia. It seems to me that a larger group of mari-timers went to our province than from any other part of Canada. Certain it is that our merchandising families, our manufacturing plants, and a great proportion of the economic background of British Columbia we owe to the maritimes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of Forestry
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
What
about the politicians?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was going to deal with them in just a moment. I will deal first with the merchants and the manufacturers who went to British Columbia. Here I am reminded of the story of the five families who first went to Hawaii, of whom it was said that they went there to do good, and instead they did well. I can assure the members in this house that that is the situation with respect to the maritimers who have gone to the province of British Columbia. They have done well. As the minister pointed out, some of them have gone into politics. As a matter of fact, a great number of them have gone into politics. Of the last nine premiers of our province, no less than four were born in the maritimes. Of the present incumbent, I might say that some of us in the province of British Columbia would like to negotiate a trade, and I rather think that we would trade him for a sack of good New Brunswick potatoes. I think it is somewhat noteworthy that the government seems to be apprised of this situation in that, they have made a great sacrifice lately in order to see that something like that is brought about. However, I want to say in addition that out of the four members of my party who were returned in the June 18 election, one of them, or one quarter, was a
maritimer.
So that we owe a tremendous debt of gratitude to the maritimes because of the flow of people from those provinces to ours. I would say to the minister that I rather think it is the loss of trained people from the historic universities and seats of learning in those great provinces to the United States, or to upper Canada, or to western Canada, that is one of the prime problems in the history of the maritimes. However, due to the development of our country, policies have had to be followed in the interests of most Canadians which have not been advantageous to the
maritimes,	and we realize that. If we go into the history of recent years and into the subsidies which have been granted, we find that the Maritime Freight Rates Act costs about $14 million per year. I think there are seven,

eight or nine million dollars worth of subsidies with regard to transportation on the waterways.
I say to the minister that we contributors from the western part of Canada and from British Columbia are quite content to assume our portion of that responsibility in respect of the bill he has brought forward at this time. I know he will not think me unkind if I say of the bill that it is nothing more than a skeleton or a letter of intent upon which he and his government have to build in the future. I hope that those of us from other parts of Canada who have made a contribution by way of taxation to the revival, the redevelopment and the rejuvenation of the maritimes might be pardoned if we are among those who in the future will be more intent upon seeing how far the minister has gone in building a muscle and a body to this skeleton which he has presented today to this house. But certainly out of the debt we owe to the maritimes we wish him and this piece of legislation well; and we propose to him that if necessary he goes on and builds it into something far greater than would appear to the people who read the bill today.
Clause 1 agreed to.
