subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE ABROAD
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing a Canadian youth service to enable qualified young Canadians to go abroad to provide scientific, technical, humanitarian and cultural assistance to peoples requiring such assistance and in particular:
(1)	To enroll volunteers in the said service qualified in scientific, professional and technical fields;
(2)	To provide for the training of volunteers in the said service;
(3)	To provide for the placement of volunteers in countries requesting such volunteers;
(4)	To provide for living allowances for volunteers while abroad and for payment of gratuities upon termination of their service.
External Affairs
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to establish a Canadian youth service to enable young Canadians to go abroad to help people in the underdeveloped countries to help themselves. A Canadian youth service would give to young Canadians an opportunity to assist people in the underdeveloped countries to wipe out poverty, ignorance and disease. Teachers, doctors, nurses, engineers, agrologists-young Canadians with professional qualifications and technical qualifications, would be enabled to go abroad and participate in what I believe is the greatest task facing the people of the world in the second half of the twentieth century, the task of raising the standard of living of the have-not countries in those parts of the world that do not enjoy the standard of living that the western countries enjoy, countries whose people live on a bare subsistence or worse than that.
I believe that young Canadians are tired of the sterile invective of the cold war. I believe they want to undertake a job that may take years, even decades, but a job that I believe has to be done. I think most members of this house would agree that it has to be done because in my opinion the people of Canada recognize a responsibility that must be discharged, a responsibility for the welfare of people all over the world, a responsibility to do whatever lies in our power to bring the standard of living of people in the underdeveloped countries up to the standard of living that is enjoyed by the people of Canada and in the other countries of the western world. I should like to repeat what President Kennedy said on the occasion of his inaugural address because I think he expressed in much better language the aspiration I have tried to express. He said:
To those peoples in the huts and villages of half the globe struggling to break the bonds of mass misery, we pledge our best efforts to help them help themselves, for whatever period is required- not because the communists are doing it, not because we seek their votes, but because it is right.
If the free society cannot help the many who are poor, it can never save the few who are rich.
We have to face the fact that in probably two thirds of the countries of the world people go to bed hungry every night. The people of these countries live without adequate shelter. They do not have the same opportunities that we in this country and in the other countries of the western world have. They can expect to die at a much earlier age than people in Canada. We have to do something about this situation.
The governments we have had have undertaken foreign aid programs, but in my view the government of this country in every case

External Affairs
has undertaken only a stunted program of foreign aid. We have never had in Canada a government with the imagination or the will to undertake an adequate program of foreign aid, a program commensurate with the capabilities of the people of Canada-the capabilities that this country has in terms of resources and manpower. This is the record, and this sorry record culminated in the decision of the present government two months ago to curtail the Colombo plan program by $8,500,000.
The United States has recognized that qualified young people have a special opportunity and are in many ways perhaps best suited to help the people in underdeveloped countries to help themselves. President Kennedy introduced legislation to establish what has become known as the peace corps, but it is important for members of the house to understand that the United States is not the only country which has undertaken a program involving the sending of young people abroad to the underdeveloped countries. Such programs have been undertaken by the Netherlands, Norway, West Germany and Belgium. In fact, the Belgian program is almost half the size of the peace corps program of the United States.
It seems to me that there is a special role for Canada to play here because the peace corps program undertaken by the United States has been determined to some extent by the exigencies of the cold war and by the special relationship which the United States has with some countries of the world. For instance, more than one quarter of the peace corps volunteers sent abroad by the United States have gone to the Philippines. At the same time the United States has sent no volunteers at all to Indonesia. It seems to me that Canada has a special role to play here. After all, Canada is bicultural. Canada is equipped to send volunteers abroad who can speak English, volunteers who can speak French and volunteers who are bilingual, speaking both languages. Because Canada has not succumbed entirely to the cold war paranoia it seems to me that young Canadians going abroad would have a much greater opportunity to help the people in underdeveloped countries than the peace corps volunteers have perhaps had, because surely the people in these countries would realize that Canadians would have no ideological axe to grind and that they were there simply to help them and not to serve any ulterior purpose.
There is no question about the need in underdeveloped countries. A survey conducted by Mr. Lewis Perinbaum, who last year was executive secretary of the Canadian

universities service overseas, found that teachers were required in practically every underdeveloped country of Africa and Asia. In fact, half of the volunteers sent abroad by the peace corps have been teachers. Doctors,, nurses and engineers are needed everywhere. Agrologists are needed in most of the countries of Africa and Asia.
There is another important category of people required in these countries, that category of people described as middle level manpower. At a conference on middle level manpower held in Puerto Rico last month, at which the Canadian government was represented, 41 countries discussed the problem of middle level manpower. Their report shows that it is not only people with professional qualifications who are required in the underdeveloped countries but people with trade skills and people equipped to teach trade skills, the kind of people who can assist in the every day tasks that we take for granted in this country, people qualified in the vocational and technical fields who can teach the people of the underdeveloped countries in these fields.
I believe that we would have to train young Canadians who were sent overseas to the underdeveloped countries in the language and the customs of the countries where they were going to work, if that were necessary. In most cases it would not really be necessary to teach them the language because Canadians are peculiarly equipped by reason of the bicultural and bilingual character of this country to go to practically every nation which requires assistance. English and French are the languages of most of the underdeveloped countries of Africa and Asia.
Young Canadians going abroad under these circumstances ought to work under local conditions. They ought to work side by side with local people and they ought to be paid by the government of this country wages or salaries equivalent to those being earned by the people with whom they are working. It seems to me that the term of their service ought to be, on the average, two years. This is the average term of service of the peace corps volunteers.
This would give to Canadians an opportunity to go abroad to assist in a high endeavour. They would return to Canada having acquired a much broader background with which to enter business, the professions or any other field of endeavour that they chose in Canada. We ought to provide that gratuities be paid to young Canadians who go abroad under these circumstances, which they would receive upon completion of their service.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the government is sending experts abroad to some of the

underdeveloped countries. I complain that the expenditure of this government on its foreign aid program is inadequate, but I realize they are sending some experts abroad. I do not propose that young Canadians going abroad as members of a Canadian youth service would attempt to duplicate the functions of these experts. Young Canadians going abroad as members of Canadian youth services would not be experts qualified to supervise the construction of a dam in Pakistan. They would be young Canadians going abroad to teach the people of the underdeveloped countries the way to perform everyday tasks that we take for granted here. For example, such things as how properly to till the fields of Africa and Asia; how to run small outpost hospitals; how to speak the English language or the French language properly; how to become acquainted with the many skills that are required in any country if the standard of living is to be raised.
I think it would be remiss to discuss a proposal such as this, to establish a Canadian youth service, without mentioning the work that has been done in this field by the Canadian universities service overseas. The universities of this country and people connected with the universities, have undertaken various programs in the last few years to send young Canadians overseas. These programs were unified with the establishment of an organization called Canadian universities service overseas about a year ago. CUSO, as it has become known, has sent volunteers overseas for the last two years. Last year they sent 16 volunteers abroad, and this year they sent 70. The fact that young Canadians are interested in this work can be established, I think, by pointing out that despite the fact CUSO had sufficient funds to send only 70 volunteers abroad, they had applications from more than 200.
If the government established a Canadian youth service, there would be no necessity to do away with CUSO or any of the other programs that have been undertaken by universities and people connected with them. I believe that a Canadian youth service could work side by side with CUSO and other programs that have been undertaken. I would go farther than that and I would suggest that the government of this country ought to supply financial assistance to CUSO and other programs that have been undertaken by the universities. In the United Kingdom, the universities have undertaken programs which entailed sending young people abroad from that country, and the government of the United Kingdom has given financial assistance for that purpose.
External Affairs
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have already suggested that a Canadian youth service would provide a great opportunity for young Canadians, an opportunity that most young Canadians do not have today. It would give them an opportunity to see other countries, to learn the customs of other countries, to acquire a knowledge of the world that I think most of us lack today. They would have the opportunity of discovering, first hand, the job that has to be done and to assist in doing that job.
It seems to me that Canada ought not to undertake a program such as this to enhance her prestige or in the pursuit of national vainglory, but rather because this is the sensible, logical thing to do in order to discharge an obligation that I suggest we in Canada have to the underdeveloped countries of the world. In talking about the job that the western countries face in assisting the people of the underdeveloped countries, Adlai Stevenson had this to say:
But it must also be done because of a much profounder reason; for it is wrong to leave children to starve who could eat with our help, wrong to let youngsters die when medical skill can save them, wrong to leave men and women without shelter, wrong to accept for others, in the midst of our own abundance, the iron pains of degrading want.
We in this country have come to recognize that we have a responsibility in respect of the people who are within the borders of this country. We recognize an obligation to make sure that our fellow Canadians do not starve, that they have adequate shelter. Surely, we ought to recognize the fact that that responsibility extends beyond our national boundaries. Surely, we ought to recognize the fact that this is a world wide responsibility, that the brotherhood of man does not end at Newfoundland or at the west coast of British Columbia. I suggest that the best way Canadians can discharge this responsibility for raising the living standards of people all over the world is to give young Canadians an opportunity to help these people. I believe this resolution would do just that. It would enable young Canadians to participate in the great task of eliminating poverty, ignorance and disease all over the world. I urge all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to give their support to this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two observations concerning not only the purpose of the measure before us but also the objective set out in the resolution by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Berger). At the outset, let me say to him that I am not in disagreement with his purpose, which is indeed worth while. It is an objective that I believe most of us, if not all of us, would support. I propose to ask, in the few minutes

External Affairs
that I intend to take, whether or not the hon. member could accomplish his purpose by this measure or whether we have already the facilities which might, in some way, provide exactly the same opportunity for young people to take part in the attempt to close the gap between the have and have-not nations of the world.
This resolution is designed basically on the very successful peace corps introduced by President Kennedy. It has been acknowledged, and I think it is generally appreciated, that while the peace corps has enjoyed some measure of success it has had certain shortcomings. Some of these are that when the scheme was first introduced these young people who went out to underdeveloped countries found they had to meet extreme hardship and in some instances were not mature enough to meet the problems which confronted them. Second, it was found some of them did not possess the qualifications or the training that was necessary in order to be of any real assistance, but when they returned to the United States they supplemented their rather academic studies by having a better understanding of the areas or countries they were visiting. The third point was that some of them psychologically were not suited for the work. It was found they were not mature enough and they did not have an understanding of some of the political and psychological problems existing in the areas to which they were sent.
However we can agree basically that the plan was successful, with perhaps a few shortcomings almost all of which have been corrected. My hon. friend suggests that we follow the same course, and before going into the details of his argument let me say I certainly wholeheartedly agree that the need for trying to close this gap between the have and have-not countries is most necessary. I hold the contention that all countries of the world should try to shift the emphasis of their aid programs from one of providing purely food, products or cash to one of improving the technical assistance they can provide so that we can help these people, who are less fortunate than ourselves, to help themselves.
I have some specific examples in mind. Just about a year ago I had the opportunity of visiting Europe, Africa and the Middle East, and in a desert in the Middle East I saw a doctor trying to treat some 550 youngsters in a clinic. The thought occurred to me that it would be a great help if one medical practitioner from Canada, perhaps as part of his post-graduate duties, were to go there and reduce the work of that Arab doctor by half. There would be great prestige for our country, in addition to the humanitarian advantages.
[Mr. Smith (Calgary South) .1
I saw much the same situation in the Congo after the Belgians had left. Many of the people there had no understanding of how to work the everyday utilities and it would have been of the greatest help had the United Nations accepted Canada's suggestion to establish a world bank of civil servants who would go into undeveloped countries after they had attained their independence to help them carry on until such time as they could employ their own technicians.
I saw much the same thing in China; but the point I wish to make is that these people require fairly highly trained technical assistance and I question whether it would be enough to send them relatively untrained youngsters, in other words, to send a boy to do a man's job.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard did not indicate the age requirement, the level of experience or the type of training which members of a youth service would be required to have. I have dealt for some years with members of youth organizations and have a great appreciation of the intelligence and ability of young people to acquire information quickly, but I would like to make the point very clear that before we embark on any program to provide technical skills for undeveloped countries we must make sure we do not send untrained young people into areas demanding qualified personnel for it would only discourage any future value of more highly trained people going into these same areas.
I think there is an area of compromise between what the hon. member has suggested and what I am about to propose, and that is that there is nothing wrong in having a group of young people out of universities taking part in Canada's present external aid program. We have already appointed a director and his first responsibility, as I recall it, is to make a survey of the talents within Canada that are surplus to our own domestic requirements, and to employ them in exactly the same manner and for the same purposes as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard now suggests. I think one of the first duties of the external affairs committee should be to make an assessment of how far this survey has been completed, because we can provide a great many of the skills required. We have a surplus of geophysicists and geologists who should be made available, under a government sponsored program, to assist many areas of the world in finding out the extent of their own natural resources.
We could ask Canadian educational institutions to provide us with trained teachers, people mature enough to go out and assist in educational programs in many of the large refugee camps and in other areas which

require improvement of their educational programs. We could also use other people from the technical trades, and here I would specifically suggest we call on the Canadian trade labour congress to assist us in developing a nucleus of these people to assist the technical trade arm of a Canadian sponsored program.
The one criticism, if it can be described as such, which can be made of the motion before us is that the program it envisages really is not ambitious enough and that it will not help the people who need help, in that it will not help them to develop their own resources. It will not help them improve their educational standards. I think it was described in terms that it would help them in everyday activities through the understanding of another language. That is of course important, but the people in these countries need help urgently in a great many other fields.
Therefore I say to the hon. member that while I would support the principle of his motion it seems to me it would be more efficient to make a further division in the external aid program of the government so that the universities, the trade labour congress and the Canadian medical profession could be called into conference to work out a program which would place greater emphasis on technical skills and making those skills available to less developed countries. Not for a moment am I taking away anything from the attributes of the young people of this country. I am merely suggesting that the magnitude of the problem must be realized by them and that they be trained to meet it.
It has been said many times that Canada has not fulfilled its responsibility in terms of foreign trade. In fact one hears various figures respecting our gross national product, or in terms of cash that it is said should represent the total amounts that we should contribute in this field to alleviate human misery. We all agree on the necessity for maintaining an active external aid program and I suggest that in the very near future we should increase the amount of moneys that are available for this purpose; but I hope it will not be done purely in cash or goods because often cash and goods are suspect. I am not speaking of Canada's contributions but of the contributions of one or two other countries.
Sometimes when these moneys and products are sent to undeveloped areas we are inclined to be a little suspicious that they do not always reach the people for whom they are destined. On the other hand it is my belief that if we provide technicians and tradesmen they will help close the gap much 27507-3-159
External Affairs
faster between the haves and the have-nots. They will help these people help themselves; and in the long run, while it is recognized that food and cash must still form part of our program, skilled tradesmen can help these people much more efficiently.
To my hon. friend who has moved this motion I say his purpose is sound but I wish he had been more ambitious. I wish he had tried to deal with the problem as it exists, and with the magnitude of it as it exists. I would suggest to him the machinery is already set up in Canada's external aid program under its director, Mr. Moran. He is a man with considerable experience who could really undertake the purpose of this motion, expand on it, and thus shift the emphasis in Canada's external aid program towards providing more technicians.
Those are the only remarks I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, with one exception. I do not think any of us need for a moment be ashamed of the contributions which this country makes in terms of mutual or external aid. I think it is recognized that we spend some $70 million a year basically in our bilateral program and through the Colombo plan. I suggest to hon. members of this house that this is not the true measurement of our external aid. We should look at the many contributions we make to the various funds and organizations within the United Nations. We should also look at the recent amendment to the export credit act extending from $200 million to $400 million the funds which are now available. I suggest also that we should look at the contribution we made recently through the world food bank. I suggest we should look at the Canadian resolutions, to which I have already referred, in an attempt to provide help to those countries which have only just recently obtained their independence. I refer to the help we have given in establishing a bank of civil servants and technicians. I suggest we should look at the contributions in a great many other fields, because the sum total of these represents more than 1 per cent of Canada's gross national product.
I believe that if one refers to any number of House of Commons papers this will be seen. The paper I have in front of me, reference No. 93 shows, if one looks at the appendix on the last page, that of the six agencies of the United Nations to which there are contributions and pledges for the voluntary special programs carried out by them, Canada is third, behind the United States and Great Britain. Having made this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to see this program still further increased. I have also indicated that I should like to see whether there has

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to present my views on this motion, express my support for the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Berger) and congratulate him upon bringing forward this motion at this time. The more particular aspect of this question to which I would like to make reference is the work of the private Canadian agencies which are now engaged in this field and to which the hon. member made some reference in introducing his motion.
The present service, as the hon. member has pointed out, is provided by the Canadian universities service overseas, known as CUSO, which is itself an amalgamation and continuation of two previously existing organizations, the Canadian overseas volunteers and the Canadian voluntary commonwealth service. Before proceeding to the discussion of the work of these two agencies and their relation to this particular motion I would like to pay tribute to the efforts of the member for York Centre in the last parliament both for his advocacy for this in this house and his very extensive efforts outside this house in advancing this very worth-while cause.
Reference has already been made to the United States peace corps. In fact, in our north American idiom the term "peace corps" has come to describe all efforts of this kind whereby young people can go and render volunteer service and make available their talents to less developed nations. It should be pointed out, however, that in addition to the nations referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the initial credit for the idea can be given to a private group in Australia which in 1952 first developed this notion of having young Australians working abroad in areas where their talents were needed. What is more, Mr. Speaker, Canadians can take some credit from the fact that, as I mentioned, due to the efforts of the former member for York Centre the Canadian overseas volunteers preceded by at least three months the foundation of President Kennedy's peace corps. These Canadian voluntary organizations now have 80 Canadian students either overseas performing functions of this kind or about to go overseas. Of this number 52 are now overseas under the auspices of CUSO, 15 under the auspices of the Canadian overseas volunteers, and five under the auspices of the Canadian voluntary commonwealth service. There are eight more to go. It is noteworthy that the

20 sent overseas by the two originating organizations have had their efforts and expenses financed by private fund raising services within this country. What is more, of the CUSO students two have been financed by private funds. The remainder have been financed by the governments of the foreign countries to which they have been sent. The cost that arises in these particular programs is that of transporting the Canadian student who has been transferred from this country to the foreign site. To give an illustration, a return ticket to Africa costs $1,300. In addition the student must be submitted to a considerable program of orientation on the language of the country to which he is going, on the customs and the nature of the duties he will have to perform there. This in turn raises the administrative overhead, so that the Canadian overseas volunteers have calculated that approximately $2,000 per student is necessary in order to get him on site.
This brings us to a problem which has arisen with these Canadian organizations. The foreign countries to which students have been sent, due largely to currency difficulties, have had difficulty in finding the exchange necessary to pay the transportation to the site. This was distressingly illustrated by the experience of CUSO in this past academic year. In May, 1.962 at the close of the academic year CUSO had no less than 200 volunteers prepared to go to sites overseas and acceptable to the organization. However, due to the difficulty in finding the means for transporting them considerable delay elapsed before they could be sent abroad and by September, due to this delay and the further uncertainties of their situation, nearly 110 of these students had dropped out. In other words this was a serious and very distressing loss of talent which could have been made available abroad.
While I support the general principle of the resolution my specific recommendation would be that the federal government should give assistance to this program by way of grants to the existing organizations. Second, I think the federal government to the greatest degree within its power should through its own facilities publicize both the availability of these services and the nature of the work that is done. The qualification which I would have regarding creating an independent governmental authority to administer this program is that I feel the universities should continue to be autonomous within this field and should administer the program. The university faculties and students are in a better position to judge the applicants coming forward, and what is more, by having it in the hands of the universities you take away any suggestion of government interference and control which in this country might tend to

discourage private contribution to the fund, and the student in the foreign country may possibly have cast upon him the stigma of being a representative of the government.
I would suggest, further, that the program should be concentrated in a number of very practical specialties wherein the immediate use of and demand for these services is very great. These are the fields of engineering, agriculture, medicine, nursing and education. We in Canada have perhaps some difficulty in appreciating just how serious is the lack of these very basic facilities in other countries. Perhaps I can illustrate this by making reference to a letter written by John Andrews, a Canadian overseas volunteer. It was written from the site on which he was working in Ceylon. Mr. Andrews writes:
My job has been mainly concerned with the next step, that of planning and arranging the construction of all the bridges and drainage culverts required as well as advising the workers with regard to any problems that they encounter.
It might be pointed out that Mr. Andrews is by professional training an engineer. He continues:
It was on a planning and inspection visit to Deriyaya-about 40 miles inland, in quite hilly country-that I was able to best see the great importance of this work. At present, the sole connecting link with the main road for two villages of 700 people each and three small tea estates, is a very rough footpath about two and a half miles long. There are two native built bridges each about 30 feet across. The walking surface consists of three bamboo poles and there is a wire slung between two high trees on to which one must hold while crossing. Of course, the sway on these structures is very great and crossing is quite hazardous. In the rainy season the river often floods and washes the bridge away. At present all the produce from the estates, all goods for the villages and even people requiring hospital care must be transported on the shoulders of bearers along this rather hazardous route.
They will build-and have already built -two reinforced concrete bridges and all the necessary drainage culverts. The project, when completed, will reduce the costs of the estate products and also of articles required by the villagers. It will open up the area and allow an easier flow of ideas and methods to a formerly isolated region, with all the benefits which this will bring to them.
I suggest there are three reasons in particular why it is to the advantage of all of us in Canada to enhance programs of this kind. First, as those who are articulate in their approach to international affairs have pointed out in recent years, Canadians are welcome in underdeveloped nations because the stigma of imperialism attaches to them less than it does to citizens of some other nations. In addition, they are not identified so readily with one side or another in the cold war. Canadians are therefore in a better position to mingle with the population and are less likely 27507-3-1594
External Affairs
to be regarded as government agents. The second reason is this: by encouraging young Canadians to mix with the foreign population we can strike a strong blow toward removing the stigma which attaches to the white man, a remaining legacy of the colonial period and one which is most difficult to remove. Third, by building up a category of young Canadians who have spent time in countries abroad on such projects as these we shall have, eventually, a group of people better capable of understanding the way of life in countries other than our own.
For all these reasons I suggest that Canadian organizations should be supported not only by government but by private sources. Therefore, while accepting the principle of the motion by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard I would suggest that federal government assistance should be given to these existing organizations rather than that a separate peace corps should be established.

Mr. Speaker, I will take only a few minutes of the time of the house to endorse, on behalf of the group I represent, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Berger).
In my opinion, the principle of the motion is excellent and completes other projects which are presently being carried out.
Thus, I know that the government itself is providing assistance to underdeveloped countries under the Colombo plan. However, I feel that this assistance, which costs us several tens of millions of dollars every year, is far from giving the results we have a right to expect.
To give only one example, recently, I had the opportunity of meeting a person who lived in those countries. Having stayed with various tribes and in various villages, that person was in a position to see the results of the assistance provided by different countries under the Colombo plan.
And he stated that money donated by the various countries to contribute to the development of those underdeveloped countries did not do much good because, in many instances, that money had been handed to those countries' administrators who used it only to increase their hold and their domination on their own people. In fact, they used it, in many instances, to build themselves palaces and to live in unheard of luxury.
On the other hand, he told me that the alms given to the missionaries of various faiths who are still in those countries, in

External Affairs
Africa as well as in South America, really bring help to those peoples.
He told me that with a dollar those missionaries could get three or even four times more than could be expected from a dollar donated through the Colombo plan.
So, it is easily understood that if we could, as Canadians, step up our assistance to church organizations of various denominations existing in those countries, our contributions out of public funds to assist the people of those underdeveloped countries would yield much better results.
In the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, I note this. He is asking the government to set up an organization to provide for the training in various trades or occupations of young people who could be needed in those countries to set up industries and schools, to assist in hospitals and at all levels of administration or social organization.
I think that our youth, in many cases, would have that vocation that would make them more or less missionaries. Because after all, it is a missionary calling, even if it is not in actual fact a religious vocation, and there are many young people whose dream has been to go to underdeveloped countries to dedicate themselves to the service of humanity, to the service of the needy who, in those countries, have been waiting for our help all those years.
I think that Canada, by stepping up its contribution through the training of young people who would, for a certain number of years, offer their services for the economic and social development of those countries, would be doing a truly humane action, an action for peace. It could even become known as a peacemaker.
We already enjoy such a reputation, but we could strengthen it, it seems to me, by sending to those countries ambassadors who would show them that our economic philosophy, far from being like that of our opponents, is based on religious and humanitarian principles that we wish to spread among all the countries of the world.
Ever since many of its countries have freed themselves from colonialism, Africa has been on the horns of a dilemma. Those countries want to improve their situation, but they lack that middle class which is the backbone of our civilized nations. They only have a poor working class, totally ignorant, plus a few 
intellectuals, trained in European countries which have helped them to study at their universities, and who come back to their own people to put in practice what they have learned and what they believe to be for the good of the nation.
But we know that, unfortunately, to be without a middle class like the one we have in our countries does create economic problems. They lack the people with the skills required to stabilize their country's economy; they lack the men capable of taking over their economy to establish industrial plants and social organizations.
That is why I say that if Canada were to take advantage of the ideas advocated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, it would be taking a significant step towards helping underdeveloped countries.
In my opinion, Canada, which has never been a colonial power, must go and repair on the spot the damage caused or left behind by colonial powers after they had gone.
We may not have any official commitment toward those countries, but we have at least some moral obligation and we should accept our responsibilities.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I feel that no member of this house would object to the government spending a greater amount of our money so that our young people may go in underdeveloped countries to help them carry out their economic recovery.
Therefore, we readily endorse the motion introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.

Mr. Speaker, I would welcome the opportunity of speaking on this motion for one hour, but I will of course not do so because under no circumstances will I talk this motion out. Therefore I will speak for only five minutes. I should like to say that four of us in this House of Commons had the opportunity and the privilege of spending some five weeks in a west African country. I wish, sir, that every member of this house could have had the same opportunity. Because if they had seen what we saw in travelling round a country the same size as British Columbia populated by 42 million people, they would without hesitation unanimously adopt the resolution now before us which has been moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Berger). Mr. Speaker, all of these newly developing countries need massive assistance. They need the assistance of engineers, technicians, doctors and scientists. They also need what we in Canada can supply, and that is volunteers among our young people who are not medical men, or scientists, or technicians.

I say, Mr. Speaker, that support of this resolution and following it through would mean a great deal.
Mr. Speaker, may I tell you of the city of Jos in northern Nigeria. In that city alone there are 70,000 people, and outside there are 200,000 in their tribal villages. There is one hospital in Jos. There is one doctor in that hospital. He looks after all the bed patients and does all the surgery. He also attends to between 600 and 800 out-patients a day from 8 o'clock in the morning until one o'clock in the afternoon. He cannot look after them all but if he had a couple of orderlies or a couple of our nurses in that hospital in Jos, would it not make a great deal of difference to the health of those people?
Let us take another city in eastern Nigeria which has perhaps one of the finest hospitals of all, and which is run by a Catholic mission. Years ago the major cause of death amongst children was lockjaw. Now they have very few deaths from lockjaw. And why? Because although two Catholic medical doctors cannot look after 500 out-patients, they can give anti-tetanus shots, and very few youngsters die now. If you go into western Nigeria, into Oyo, Ibadan and Ife, these shots are not given and lockjaw is one of the great causes of death. Some of our young Canadians who have been trained as orderlies, nurses or technicians could provide such a service, under medical supervision.
In that country of 42 million people there are 83 doctors. Midwifery is hardly known. Most times when children are born the umbilical cord is cut too long. So how is it closed? I wish the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) were here to back up what I say. It is closed with a dab of goat, camel or cow dung. And what happens? Infection. One child out of two dies. What could some of our young people do? With two or three years of the training we give in Canada they could help people under these circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I have just given you a couple of dramatic illustrations showing why I should like to talk on this topic for an hour, and why I am so wholeheartedly in support of this motion; but I will call it quits now so that we can have a vote and it is not talked out.

Is the minister going to stand here and tell us that five people on a part time basis are going to be able to do the job that a whole region of Canada is demanding? Atlantic Development Board can give full time attention to the problems about which he and other hon. members of this house have spoken.

Because clause 14 gives powers to other than those representatives elected by the provincial governments. It is the technical, the scientific, the practical and the economic part of this bill. Atlantic Development Board
The board may engage on a temporary basis or for any period of not more than two years the services of persons having technical or specialized knowledge of any matters relating to the work of the board...
I suggest that if this bill is to have the sort of consideration I hope it will have, we must put together not only clause 3 and clause 9, but also clause 14. That precedent has been well established by the Minister of Justice. But as I think the question is a proper one some kind of legal opinion should be forthcoming. The phrase "during good behaviour" is used in all statutes. It is part of the technique of good draftsmanship and it means precisely what it says, that a man shall hold office during good behaviour.
The courts on one occasion have said that a person appointed to serve as a member of a workmen's compensation board could not be said to have complied with the requirement of "good behaviour" when, outside of the office which he occupied, in a speech having to do with the administration of the workmen's compensation board he complained about the administration of the board of which he was a member. The courts held he acted contrary to the standard of "during good behaviour." This is a demonstration of the meaning. It is apparent since this legislation was in the resolution stage and has been given considerable publicity that this is one of those emergency measures of which the government spoke so frequently, otherwise I presume it would not be before the house before Christmas. I wonder whether the government has in fact already inquired of suitable people as to whether they might find a chairman, and whether $3,000 a year would be sufficient for anyone who is qualified; or has the government, following its usual practice, decided that amongst those defeated Conservative members of the 1958 parliament there may be someone who wishes a greater honorarium and they have thus decided, without being able to say to whom they will give the job, that they require a blank cheque from parliament in order that they may pay it to the person who offers to come for the least amount of money? I have not been very long in the house. This is the first time I have been asked to give a blank cheque in order that a position might be filled. Surely the minister must have some idea of what will be required to pay any individual who undertakes this function. I suggest the committee should not be asked to give the government a blank cheque with respect to this amendment and, if asked, that it should never consent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: This amendment was introduced by the Minister of Fisheries. Surely the committee is entitled to hear from him the real reasons or justification for this amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: During the course of the debate there has been some objection, I believe, to limiting the salary which is proposed for the chairman of this important board. There have been some remarks made in the committee tonight, some by the hon. member for Niagara Falls and by the hon. member for Cape Breton South which are, in my opinion, unworthy of the hon. members concerned. They implied, for example, that ladies and gentlemen of this country who have a deep sense of public service and who have often at great inconvenience to themselves, offered to stand for parliament are in some mysterious way thereby reduced in the public esteem to some category which would not allow them to serve on any public board. That sort of attitude is, in my humble opinion, contemptible, and it reflects very badly on the thinking of those who make such statements. We are Canadians, and there are many people in this country who were proud to serve this nation in various capacities. During the war, for example, there were hundreds of Canadians who served for a dollar a year.

I shall be glad to withdraw that remark if, by making it, I cast inadvertently any reflection on any woman who served during world war II. But I want to say this: during the war many Canadians served for a dollar a year. There are many citizens of the maritime provinces who are deeply concerned with serving their area in particular, and it is quite possible that someone might come forward who did not wish to receive any remuneration except a nominal one. On the other hand, it might be advisable to provide a fairly substantial salary. This is a matter to be left to the governor in council.
As far as the point raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is concerned, the resolution already passed by this house does not limit in any way the amount which might be provided, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already pointed out. That, in a few words, is my understanding of why this amendment has been made. That is my reason for moving it

-so that there may be flexibility in this regard; so that there may be some variation depending on circumstances.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think those of us who have followed the debate in the resolution stage and on the bill itself thus far have been impressed by the way the minister has conducted himself as the spokesman for the government. But I think tonight he has not done himself justice, nor has he lived up to the high standard which he had set for himself in the period preceding tonight's discussion.
To say to this committee now, that the government has no idea what the salary of the chairman is to be, to suggest that the government is not clear about the amount of time the chairman will spend in the discharge of his duties, to remind us that the minister is not clear as to the kind of person he has in mind, is to establish without any doubt that we are justified in assuming that, notwithstanding what was desired, this bill is nothing more than a fagade, that this bill does not represent the endeavour which the minister said was his in seeking to provide an instrument to deal with the serious economic problems which face the Atlantic provinces.
In clause 4 and all the subclauses thereof it is provided that not one member of the board, including the chairman, will be expected to spend his full time in the discharge of his duties. I hope it is not contrary to our rules to refer to bills which are not yet before us-no exception was taken when my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition spoke a few moments ago. But it will be found that in the other bill which is shortly to be discussed in this house the chairman is expected to spend his full time in the prosecution of the assignment given him, for the simple reason that it is not possible to discharge such an obligation unless he does devote his full time to the assignment. The government claims this Atlantic development board is to serve a useful and substantial purpose. If the minister says to us, as he has indicated, that it is not yet determined how much the chairman will receive, that it is not yet determined how much time he will spend in the discharge of the duties assigned in clause 9, then it is clear that this bill is not intended to do the job which well meaning members of this house, notwithstanding their criticism, have assumed was the intention behind this measure.
The Atlantic provinces face some serious problems. They have the highest level of unemployment of any region in our country -a greater percentage of unemployment in the work force. Is it to be assumed that this
Atlantic Development Board problem is going to be corrected by a chairman whose salary is indeterminate, by a chairman who will not be expected to spend his full time in the discharge of his obligations? Surely the minister does not want us to persist in pointing out the absurd position into which he has been driven as a result of the uncertain policy which apparently, his colleagues have imposed on him in their unwillingness to state in this clause how much is to be paid to the chairman. Surely the minister now has in mind who is to be the chairman. Surely he knows how much that person is worth. Surely he knows that that person will be able to work X number of hours. I would contend that if this job is to be done properly he should devote his full time to it, and that he should be well remunerated for so doing.
The history of this clause is revealing. Hon. gentlemen, when confronted with this subsection, noted that the chairman was to receive only $3,000. They concluded, and I think quite properly, that if a man was going to be paid only $3,000 a year, he could not possibly be expected to spend his full time at the job, and that if he did not he was not the kind of person to whom should be entrusted the responsibility which is being provided for under this act. I say to the minister that he has handled this bill, in my judgment, as adroitly and efficiently as any member of this government has been able to demonstrate his or her capacity so to do, but he does not do himself justice when he allows himself to let rest the explanation which he gives. One might expect that kind of explanation from the Minister of Justice, but one would not expect that the present minister with his experience as head of a provincial government and with the sincerity which obviously he had when he introduced this measure, would give this sort of explanation. I appeal to him to take the house into his confidence. When the government formed this board, in concept at any rate, it must have had in mind the kind of chairman it wanted. It must have had in mind an outstanding person, I presume in the Atlantic provinces, one who knows the Atlantic provinces, who is aware of the problems facing the fishermen, the farmers, and those engaged in the factories and the universities, the kind of person who could represent the four different provincial regions. That kind of person obviously must be a man of considerable competence. We ask the minister to tell us whether or not this bill was drawn up simply because the government was hard put to demonstrate that it had a program to meet the problems, which are now of an emergent character, and that it was not resorting to this particular technique-as has been done

Mr. Chairman, I always appreciate the interventions of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. They always consist of single sentences which are so incomprehensible that even on reflection and upon re-reading they are not understood by himself.
The Minister of Fisheries said that it may be that the analogy of the dollar-a-year man will apply, and that perhaps someone who does not need assistance or remuneration by the crown will take on this responsibility as a voluntary assignment. I am sure that there are many people in the Atlantic provinces who are capable of fitting in with this concept which the Minister of Fisheries has in mind. But in such an event there would be no difficulty in such person returning the salary which might be given under this bill to such a chairman.
The minister said that the bill is intended to represent a serious endeavour; that it is an attempt to provide the government with an advisory body to deal with the fundamental economic problems which face the Atlantic provinces. If that is the case I suggest that the minister take this subsection back to his colleagues and tell them he is embarrassed by the explanation they have caused him to make tonight. Then let him come back and tell us that he has in mind somebody who will spend his full time on the job, who will be paid a salary adequate to the demands which will be made upon him. No explanation less than this will satisfy this house. No explanation less than this will satisfy the Atlantic provinces. Anything less than this will be evidence of an intention on
the part of the government to introduce in this bill something that looks good in form but which is not capable, in its very wording and provisions, of doing anything substantial to help the Atlantic area.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the observations made by the hon. member for Essex East are not the observations that one would expect from someone who had read the bill through. If the hon. member would read the bill he would find that the executive director is the full time servant of the board. It was never necessarily intended that the chairman would be full time. If he has not taken the trouble to read the bill, then I am not responsible for his lack of perception. But he himself is responsible if he has not read the bill through and is not familiar with all its details. I would say this to him, that I am not particularly worried about how the people of the Atlantic provinces will take this bill.
